top_three.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
top_three.title_en: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs

top_three.summary_en: Character.ai, currently under Chapter 11 bankruptcy, intends to auction sensitive data from 21 million users, including 2.1 million minors, to Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. A coalition of 42 state attorneys general, led by California AG Rob Bonta and Connecticut AG William Tong, is challenging this move, citing breaches of privacy commitments and potential violations of state chatbot safety laws effective January 2027.
paragraphs: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)

top_three.title_en: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future

top_three.summary_en: Google's 'My Channel' patent details a system that utilizes user demographic, geolocation, and viewing history to generate personalized AI-driven video feeds. The technology includes concepts for creating digital avatars of users to feature them as protagonists in AI-generated narrative content.
paragraphs: Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.

According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.

Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.

My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.

When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

topic_focus.title_zh: 美政界图谋《国防生产法》强行干预英伟达黄仁勋去留
topic_focus.title_en: US Officials Floated Using Wartime Law to Reappoint Nvidia CEO Huang
topic_focus.summary_zh: 华盛顿邮报披露特朗普政府官员曾研讨引用《国防生产法》以施压英伟达董事会重聘黄仁勋。尽管司法部随后排除了黄仁勋的国家安全风险，但此举揭示了美国政府为确保AI关键产能，已将半导体巨头高层人事视为国家战略博弈的最高优先级，引发市场对企业自主权的极度担忧。
topic_focus.summary_en: Washington Post reports US officials considered using the Defense Production Act to force Nvidia to reappoint CEO Jensen Huang. While the DOJ later cleared Huang of national security risks, this blatant move to treat a tech firm’s C-suite as a strategic asset signals a new era of state intervention in critical AI hardware supply chains.

perspective_pro.speaker_zh: 美联邦防务及情报官员
perspective_pro.point_zh: AI芯片不仅是商品，更是数字时代的能源。为了维护国家AI领先地位，政府必须确保最强算力领导者与国家意志协同一致。
perspective_pro.point_en: AI chips are the energy of the digital age. Ensuring the alignment of hardware leadership with national interest is a prerequisite for maintaining AI supremacy.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 华尔街分析师与硅谷投资者
perspective_con.speaker_en: Wall Street Analysts & Silicon Valley Investors
perspective_con.point_zh: 政治干预企业人事是商业逻辑的灾难。这种激进的战时行政手段会引发资本恐慌，削弱英伟达作为全球创新标杆的合规性与中立地位。
perspective_con.point_en: Political interference in corporate governance is a catastrophe for business logic. This aggressive use of wartime powers threatens to undermine market confidence and Nvidia's neutral global standing.

topic_focus.summary_zh: Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪公开驳斥了关于“人类应向AI让渡自由意志”的内部言论，直指同行高管沉迷于“基于共鸣(vibes-based)”的营销定位。这一表态揭开了主流AI公司在社会治理边界与技术宿命论上的深层意识形态裂痕。
topic_focus.summary_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly rejected the notion of surrendering human free will to AI systems, criticizing rival executives for engaging in 'vibes-based' posturing. This clash reveals a widening ideological rift among top AI leaders regarding the role of synthetic intelligence in societal governance and decision-making.

perspective_pro.point_zh: AI应作为人类认知的增强工具而非替代者。阿莫迪强调人类主体性是AI部署的前提，而非可以随模型能力提升而折价的筹码。
perspective_pro.point_en: AI should serve as an augmentation tool, not a replacement. Amodei insists human agency is a non-negotiable prerequisite for deployment, regardless of model scale.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 穆斯塔法·苏莱曼等行业同行
perspective_con.point_zh: 质疑阿莫迪口号式声明的虚伪性。认为在追求AGI的竞赛中，所谓伦理护栏在极高的商业利益下缺乏有效的数学与制度约束。
perspective_con.point_en: Skeptics argue that slogans are not guardrails. They contend that in the race for AGI, ethical proclamations lack real-world mathematical or institutional constraints.

news.title: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
news.title_en: Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs
news.author: Sarah Perez
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Character.ai, currently under Chapter 11 bankruptcy, intends to auction sensitive data from 21 million users, including 2.1 million minors, to Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. A coalition of 42 state attorneys general, led by California AG Rob Bonta and Connecticut AG William Tong, is challenging this move, citing breaches of privacy commitments and potential violations of state chatbot safety laws effective January 2027.
paragraphs: What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)

news.content_snippet:
Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the company’s blog:

Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.

When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window ins
news.summary_en: Anthropic has launched the 'Install as app' beta for Mac and Windows, allowing users to package Claude Artifacts into standalone desktop applications. Based on an Electron shim, these apps require the main Claude process to handle model interactions and system permissions, with files localized and indexed for OS-native integration.

news.title: Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
news.title_en: Hegseth, Pentagon officials floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
news.author: Elizabeth Dwoskin, Tara  Copp, Nancy Cook, and Natalie Allison
news.content_snippet:
As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea: invoking a Cold War-era law to pressure Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the debate.

The Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that grants the president broad authority to intervene in the economy, has historically been used to mobilize private companies to supply the military in wartime or durin
news.summary_en: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Steve Feinberg explored invoking the 1950 Defense Production Act to pressure Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. The move was motivated by the administration’s perception of Nvidia as a national security pillar essential for maintaining dominance in the AI arms race against China.
paragraphs: As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea: invoking a Cold War-era law to pressure Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the debate.

The Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that grants the president broad authority to intervene in the economy, has historically been used to mobilize private companies to supply the military in wartime or during national emergencies. The first Trump administration used the law to prompt General Motors to produce ventilators during the covid-19 pandemic.

Before Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced Monday, Pentagon officials including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure Nvidia’s board to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive talks.
News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

While the law provides no clear path to installing a new CEO, it could be used as a warning. “Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” said one of the three people, a Trump administration official. That could have curbed the chipmaker’s production plans and profit.

The conversation about the law as part of a campaign to place Huang back in power, which has not been previously reported, reflects the intensity with which the military views the AI race with China and the lengths the Trump administration may be willing to go to intervene in the economy. It also reveals another dimension of the Defense Department’s growing entanglement with Silicon Valley: Though the DPA has never been used to install a leader in a private company, the idea has gained currency with some influential members of the tech sector in recent weeks.

It is unclear what was ultimately conveyed to Nvidia, or whether those arguments made their way to President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, both of whom ultimately became convinced that Huang needed to be back in his job. The two were willing to use the powerful muscle of the federal government to make that happen, as part of a “full-court press” by Cabinet officials over the weekend, one of the people said. Hegseth and Feinberg were part of that campaign, according to two of the people.

Government officials emphasized during the talks that restoring Huang was important for U.S. national security, but Nvidia’s board did not perceive it as a threat, according to a person familiar with the board’s thinking.

The president and vice president came to believe in the importance of Nvidia to the economy and its leader’s singular ability to stabilize financial markets, said two other people familiar with the discussions, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to describe them.
Trump personally asked Vance to become involved in brokering the restoration of the embattled CEO as the scandal dragged down the stock market. Huang returned to Nvidia on Monday morning.
The White House referred questions about the strategy to the Pentagon.

“The conversations described between DOW senior leaders never happened and no such proposal was made by the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, or Under Secretary,” said a Pentagon official who refused to be named. (DOW refers to the Department of War, the administration’s preferred name for the Defense Department.)

Lenders are reassessing exposure to facilities serving Chinese firms, including Bridge Data Centres, Digital Halo, and Aolani, due to heightened regulatory uncertainty.

While Jensen Huang's surprise return to Nvidia Corp. buoyed AI stocks briefly earlier this week, bankers remained concerned about the legal risks of financing data centers and neoclouds potentially facing stricter US export controls. Deals that were near the finish line are suddenly in doubt and lenders trying to sell down their exposure are struggling to find interested buyers.

Some lenders have delayed moving forward as they do more due diligence on an upsized $6.6 billion loan sought by Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres, whose Malaysian facilities are used by clients including Bytedance, according to people involved in the discussions. Bain referred questions to BDC, which declined to comment. Bytedance did not respond to a request for comment.

One bank has decided to pass on a fully underwritten $372 million loan for Partners Group-backed Digital Halo, while others are asking more questions, people familiar with those talks said. The funds are for a data center in Malaysia that services Alibaba and other customers, they said. Multiple banks were also reassessing a $480 million loan for Aolani, a Singapore-based neocloud that gets business from Bytedance, separate people familiar said last week.
Digital Halo, Aolani and Alibaba didn't respond to questions. Partners Group declined to comment.

The Biden administration's 2022 export restrictions on advanced US chips spawned an ecosystem of companies in Southeast Asia to help Chinese technology firms access the coveted hardware remotely. Lending to data centers in the region surged in the following years, while chip financing was just beginning to take off more recently as banks got more comfortable with the riskier deals.

That changed after the US announced last week that companies in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil will need a US government license to purchase advanced AI chips from American manufacturers. Globally, data centers that already lease significant compute to Chinese firms will need a separate license to continue doing so and have a 90-day window to obtain it.

More than a dozen bankers said their teams were waiting for answers on how the new curbs would affect borrowers and that would at the very least delay potential deals from going through. Lenders including Citigroup Inc. and Standard Chartered Plc, as well as Singapore's major banks, have launched a sweeping review of data center clients, people familiar with the matter said earlier.

Some banks are looking to reduce certain exposure to AI and data center debt, including through secondary loan sales and so-called significant risk transfers. Singapore's United Overseas Bank Ltd. is seeking a SRT deal of around $1 billion to offload risks tied to data center and infrastructure loans among other sectors, people familiar with the matter said. But the current news headlines are slowing progress, one of them said, adding that details are not firmed up and could change.
A representative for UOB declined to comment, citing deal confidentiality.

Private lenders, who were the most aggressive in seeking out the higher returns associated with GPU financing, are also growing more cautious. At least one fund has decided not to participate in a $300 million loan to GMI Cloud, an Nvidia cloud partner, to fund chips for a Thai data center that would be used by Tencent, according to a person familiar with the matter.
GMI Cloud and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment.

news.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
news.title_en: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
news.author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
news.content_snippet:
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a p
news.summary_en: Google's 'My Channel' patent details a system that utilizes user demographic, geolocation, and viewing history to generate personalized AI-driven video feeds. The technology includes concepts for creating digital avatars of users to feature them as protagonists in AI-generated narrative content.
paragraphs: Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.

According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.

Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.

My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.

When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

The investors, led by

paragraphs: Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA) has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a long-running US investor lawsuit accusing the chipmaker of misleading shareholders about the role crypto mining played in its gaming business.

The proposed settlement follows a lawsuit filed in 2018 by investors who claimed Nvidia failed to properly disclose how much of its graphics processing unit (GPU) revenue came from crypto miners rather than video game players, according to a court filing on Tuesday,

The investors, led by Stockholm-based asset manager E. Ohman J:or Fonder AB, argued that Nvidia presented strong gaming revenue as evidence of demand from gamers while a significant portion of sales was driven by crypto mining.

The case centers on Nvidia's sales during the 2017 crypto boom, when rising prices for Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO: $ETH) encouraged miners to buy large numbers of powerful GPUs.
Although Nvidia introduced graphics cards specifically designed for crypto mining, investors alleged that miners also purchased GeForce gaming GPUs, helping drive reported gaming revenue higher.

The issue became more apparent in 2018, when crypto prices fell and demand for mining hardware weakened. Nvidia subsequently lowered its revenue forecast, citing a sharp decline in crypto-related demand and excess inventory of gaming GPUs. The company's shares also came under pressure after the news.

news.content_snippet:
WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken an
news.summary_en: US Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang poses no national security risk without conducting a formal investigation, relying on findings from probe into clients like Super Micro and Megaspeed. This decision facilitated Huang's reinstatement by the Trump administration, despite bipartisan Congressional pushback demanding more rigorous scrutiny ahead of his scheduled testimony.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Jensen Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as Nvidia chief executive this week, despite active probes into the chipmaker’s customers and allegations he conducted an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, Attorney General Todd Blanche concluded that there was no evidence the tech titan had broken any laws based on the Justice Department’s ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

That determination, which is subject to change as the probes continue, was crucial to Blanche’s decision to tell Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend that he possessed no evidence that Huang posed a risk to national security, said two of the people.

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement has angered members of Congress — both Republicans and Democrats — who say it’s too soon to set aside questions about whether Nvidia or its CEO endangered US national security. The lack of any additional effort to examine their roles prior to Trump’s intervention will likely fuel a push for more investigations on Capitol Hill.
Huang is due to testify next week.

The Justice Department probes of Nvidia customers found no evidence that Huang was acting as an agent of China or knowingly transferred sensitive semiconductor technology or information to China, the two people said. Nvidia was not a target of those investigations and cooperated, providing documents, interviews and other data that helped lead to that conclusion, they added.

There was also no counterintelligence probe of Huang himself. US spy agencies have gathered information on Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and alleged paramour of Jensen Huang suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, said two other people familiar with the effort. But the US had no details that would warrant a probe into the Nvidia CEO, they said.
Counterintelligence investigations are run separately from criminal investigations and are aimed at monitoring and neutralizing national security threats, rather than building a case for indictment.

Justice Department officials concluded that Nvidia and Huang had committed no wrongdoing and did not suspect its chief executive posed a national-security risk, two of the people familiar with the matter said.
Trump and Vance conveyed that conclusion to Nvidia’s board, which decided to reinstate Huang, according to Trump’s account of events in a CNBC interview on Monday.
Speaking to reporters in Ohio on Wednesday, Vance said Justice Department and national security officials told him that Huang was not the subject of an investigation prior to his reinstatement.

“We were told that he was under no investigation,” he said, adding that he didn’t think Trump would need to pardon Huang because he had not broken the law. “I haven’t seen any evidence again that he committed a crime.”

news.summary_en: Restrictions on remote access to advanced chips and anti-distillation defenses from US-based model providers are widening the development gap between Chinese AI labs and US incumbents. Estimates from DeepSeek indicate a potential nine-month lag without distillation, forcing firms like Moonshot AI and Alibaba to pivot toward domestic silicon and intensified internal RL research.
paragraphs: The US is tightening its grip in the AI race with China, and the push is already having an effect, according to The Information. Chinese AI developers including Deepseek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba have been under pressure since September, squeezed by restrictions on Chinese firms' remote access to advanced Nvidia chips in foreign data centers and by successful anti-distillation measures from OpenAI and Anthropic.

As a result, many ongoing projects are facing delays, the report says. Last month, Deepseek researchers internally estimated that their gap to top US models could grow from three to six months to nine months if distillation disappears completely. Moonshot AI has already canceled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia.

Chinese firms are now looking for new workarounds, the publication reports. Some are trying to rent computing power through non-Chinese third parties, while companies such as MiniMax, Mihoyo, and Alibaba are leaning more heavily on domestic chips. They are also investing more in training data for their own reinforcement learning.

news.summary_en: Meta's WhatsApp has launched a global message scheduling feature, allowing users to schedule texts, images, and videos between 10 minutes and 14 days in advance via a long-press on the send button. The messages will execute even while the device is offline, closing the utility gap with Telegram and Signal.
paragraphs: WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats.

The feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later.
Users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message.
Notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos.

The feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams.
WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out.

news.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
news.title_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says letting AI govern society would be "a bad idea"
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.summary_en:
Dario Amodei said it was "absurd"to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will"to AI systems.

In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control.

AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes,"Amodei wrote. Political decisions should stay
paragraphs: Dario Amodei said it was "absurd"to suggest he believed people should "surrender human free will"to AI systems.

In a lengthy post on X, he responded to an Axios report that cited people familiar with internal discussions. The outlet reported that some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems, and often should, rather than fight for control.

AI must be governed by "legitimate democratic processes,"Amodei wrote. Political decisions should stay in human hands, he argued, and he rejected handing power to AI as firmly as he rejected autocracy.

[...] We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination on the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word to governance by AI, and I feel just as strongly that handing over governance to AI is a bad idea. Dario Amodei
Automating specific tasks such as driving, developing cancer drugs, and writing software could benefit humanity, Amodei said, but that was a different matter from giving up free will in politics.
### Amodei says that full automation isn't always worth the risk

End-to-end automation could also bring risks, Amodei wrote, including serious job disruption and AI building new models without human oversight. "It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,"he wrote. "But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it."In many cases, he added, "humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better."

Amodei said AI companies didn't differ much on automating specific tasks. Some AI CEOs, he wrote, repeated slogans like "human control and agency"and "AI should be just a tool"but still shipped products built for more and more automation.

Anthropic, by contrast, refused to allow its existing models to be used for autonomous weapons during its dispute with the Pentagon. He was "willing to risk Anthropic's future as a company"over that refusal, "even in the face of legal sanctions,"Amodei wrote.
subheadings: Amodei says that full automation isn't always worth the risk

news.title: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
news.title_en: 1Password said hackers broke into its internal systems, but customer passwords are safe
news.author: Zack Whittaker
news.summary_en:
Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee
paragraphs: Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company said in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

The attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the company’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

1Password said that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.
In addition, the company said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.
It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the company has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll update if we hear back from 1Password.

The company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

paragraphs: ElevenLabs is in early talks for a funding round at a $33B valuation, planned for the first quarter of 2027, Bloomberg reported. That would be 50% above its $22B valuation in September, and its annual recurring revenue has reached $700M, one person said.

ElevenLabs is in early talks to raise money at a $33B valuation, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The voice AI company plans to start the round in the first quarter of 2027, though some investors want it to begin sooner.
That would be a 50% jump from the $22B ElevenLabs was valued at in a $300M share sale in September. It also fits the company’s habit of setting valuations in multiples of 11, a nod to its name.
ElevenLabs’ annual recurring revenue has reached $700M, one person told Bloomberg, up from the $600M it reported in September. ElevenLabs declined to comment.

The price would be steep next to its peers. London video AI firm Synthesia was valued at $4B in January with about $140M in yearly revenue. Mistral was valued at €21B in September, having passed $400M early in the year.
Investors may be spurred on by Anthropic’s record $107.3B IPO, which brought early backers huge gains.

ElevenLabs was founded in London in 2022 by Mati Staniszewski and Piotr Dabkowski, and makes realistic AI voices for games, audiobooks and AI agents. Staniszewski has said it could start preparing for an IPO in 2028.

news.title_en: Backblaze explains why it’s sharing customer information with advertisers
news.author: Scharon Harding
news.summary_en:
Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze’s privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.

Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Inte
paragraphs: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze’s privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.

Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”

The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

On December 1, a new privacy policy takes effect. It includes a table listing the types of “general personal information” that Backblaze says it has been collecting and sharing with third parties, including “advertising and marketing partners” since December 1, 2025, This information includes identifiers (such as “name, address, Internet Protocol address, [and] email address”); commercial information (such as “records of personal property, products or services purchased, obtained, or considered, or other purchasing or consuming histories or tendencies”; geolocation data that “can be used to determine a device’s physical location”; and “sensory or surveillance data” (which includes “call recordings or other audio, electronic, or visual monitoring or surveillance”).

This has concerned some users, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:

The Privacy Policy table lists one set of recipients across all data categories, which is why it can read differently. Our legal team will review the table for clarity as part of our next review cycle.
### No “sensitive personal information” shared

Notably, no “sensitive personal information,” such as social security numbers, credit card numbers, or “precise geolocation,” is shared with advertisers, the policy states. However, identifiers, commercial information, “Internet or Other Similar Network Activity,” and “geolocation data” may be “sold or shared for targeted Advertising”

Critically, the upcoming policy “only applies to the information collected in respect of your account and not to the content that you store on our system.” Backblaze’s broader terms of service also state that: “Files stored using Backblaze Computer Backup are encrypted prior to being sent to us.”

However, some customers remain concerned that the privacy policy doesn’t more clearly and distinctly explain that Backblaze won’t share or sell content from customers’ backup files. In response, Backblaze’s representative explained:

This is because the Privacy Notice’s sale and sharing disclosures relate to website and marketing data, such as information collected through cookies and similar technologies on our site. They do not apply to files customers store with us.
Renatta Siewert, Backblaze’s director of communications and brand programs, reiterated to Ars that Backblaze doesn’t share the contents of backup or storage files with advertisers:

news.title: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
news.title_en: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
news.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz
news.summary_en:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.

Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.

Jack Duhamel
paragraphs: Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.

Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.

Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.

The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.

The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
### Scrutiny over Chinese access to Nvidia chips
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.

The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action,"sources previously told CNBC.

In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box"on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."

paragraphs: OpenAI is testing a new feature called "Private Inference"that lets companies run queries on its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to access the data. CEO Sam Altman said the company is now piloting the previously announced offering with its first enterprise customers. Better privacy makes AI useful for a much wider range of work, Altman wrote.

Shekar, the OpenAI employee leading the effort, called it a first step toward "private intelligence for everyone."OpenAI is currently scaling up the compute capacity needed to expand the offering. For now, Private Inference targets business customers, whose data OpenAI already doesn't use for training. Consumer ChatGPT conversations, by contrast, are used for training by default unless users opt out.

With Private Inference, queries are processed on specially isolated hardware whose security can be independently verified, according to OpenAI. Altman also pointed to Private Safety Processing, a system that lets OpenAI scan for abuse without storing customer data. Flagged content is encrypted and stored in the customer's own cloud, and only a secured review system can read it. Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute.

news.title_en: Every raises $17.5 million at $110 million valuation, betting venture-backed media can work
news.author: Allie Garfinkle
news.summary_en:
Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

paragraphs: Ask Dan Shipper how often venture-backed media startups succeed, and he’s candid.

“My feeling about the history of media companies taking venture capital is that it doesn’t go very well,” he said. In other words, it usually doesn’t work out, I suggest. “It works out never, actually,” laughs Shipper, founder of AI-focused media and software company Every.

Shipper’s right: VC-backed media startups of yesteryear have frequently tanked in spectacular fashion, from The Messenger and Vice to Ozy Media and Quibi. But Shipper is betting that Every—currently with about 130,000 unpaid subscribers and almost 10,000 paid—can play by its own rules and ultimately win its own game.

Hence, the fundraise: Every recently raised $17.5 million in Series A funding, at a $110 million post-money valuation, Fortune has exclusively learned. IA Ventures’s Jesse Beyroutey led the round, with Betaworks and The Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson joining, among others. Shipper, 35, will retain full control of the company, and is changing his title to “Philosopher King,” which I rib him about. He good-naturedly says the change is semiotic.

“The really important thing about taking the money for me was that we’d do it in a way that allows us to achieve our goals… and do it in a way that doesn’t require us to sacrifice our soul or the things about the company that I love deeply,” said Shipper. “I think of changing my title as a symbolic thing. If this was a normal venture capital deal, that would be completely off the table and ridiculous.”

And this isn’t a normal venture deal, in a couple of ways. First, Every is a media company. With its neoclassical pop art aesthetic, Every has a multi-pronged business model: Its writing serves a professional audience seeking to become “AI-native,” while the 35-person company also provides consulting services to large companies and produces conferences (I recently interviewed Shipper at Every’s Thesis: 2027 conference in Brooklyn). Second, Shipper didn’t raise in a standard startup process: IA’s Beyroutey and Shipper are close friends (they went to college together) and Shipper went straight to Beyroutey.

“I didn’t shop the deal,” said Shipper. “I went to someone I deeply trust, who understands the business deeply, who understands exactly what I want to do with it, and has put me in the position where I make all the decisions to build the company in the way that I want to build it,” Shipper said. “I think that’s the only way to build a business like this, because this is a very unique shape. It’s a media company and a technology company, kind of smushed together.”

Shipper started Every in 2020, about six years after exiting his first startup, co-browsing company Firefly, in 2014 (the acquisition came right as he was graduating college). He spent the intervening years finding the right next thing. Every became the answer, in part because it addressed a number of questions that Shipper had been asking throughout his life. For one, he’d long felt tension between writing and entrepreneurship (at Every he could be both). He’d also been interested in tech since he was a kid.

“I thought a lot about why Microsoft and Windows had worked, and one of the big reasons is that they came during a hardware platform shift, from mainframes to PCs,” said Shipper. “They started building operating systems for that, and that’s always a really big opportunity…. And I thought: I wonder what my platform shift is going to be?”
Shipper and Every are all-in on AI, and the company is built to help people understand how they can actually use AI, in their jobs and their lives.

“I think too few companies are trying to do that,” said Shipper. “Too many companies are trying to build the machine god or are worrying about Armageddon, and I’m not…. I would expect improvements we’re seeing [in AI] to continue, and I would expect there to be a gap between the improvements that you see on the charts and how well those improvements translate into actually better work by people (and that people at companies are proud of). Our job is to fill that gap.”
Shipper is optimistic that AI won’t replace humans at work, a common fear and feature of AI discourse.

news.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
news.title_en: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
news.author: Emma Roth
news.summary_en:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satel
paragraphs: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.

The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.

SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.

Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

paragraphs: The FCC on Wednesday granted the first authorization ever for a constellation of data centers in space — a win for Elon Musk and his SpaceX operation that comes less than two years after his role as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency under President Trump.
The authorization sees the Commission approve SpaceX’s deployment of 1 million orbital compute modules “to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth.”
And, the Carr Commission proclaims, “it promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization—one that can harness the full power of the sun.”
The system also operates consistent with the FCC’s orbital debris rules.

In a statement, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said, “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth. Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”

With data centers a divisive topic across the U.S. in a wide range of communities, including Nashville, where a proposed center adjacent to the city’s zoo generated a vociferous round of protests in June, the idea of putting them in space could supercharge a company already seen by Wall Street as a potential disruptor to the cellular telephone industry. Already, T-Mobile has seen its stock price fall by $50 a share from earlier this year thanks to SpaceX efforts. On November 25, Microsoft shares were down to the low $480s after recently climbing above $500 per share.

paragraphs: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.

We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.
### Why migrate?

We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.
#### Incremental or all at once?

Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)

The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.

As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.

news.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
news.title_en: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
news.author: Casey Crownhart
news.summary_en:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just on
paragraphs: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

paragraphs: Amazon and Meta are in talks to end the block on Meta's AI shopping agent Muse in Amazon's online store. In September, Amazon blocked Muse's access. Ad revenue and control over search results are the main sticking points in the ongoing talks, Fortune reports. Amazon worries that shopping agents like Muse could weaken its relationship with customers and bypass the ads on its platform, a business that brings in $68.6 billion a year.

Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, said shopping through third-party agents so far hasn't been more convenient or better than going directly to a retailer, but he didn't rule out opening access. The company also offers its own agentic shopping features, which in some cases have pulled in sellers that don't sell on Amazon. It previously tried and failed to block Perplexity. Any deal would need sign-off from both CEOs, according to Fortune.

Muse is Meta's most successful consumer AI product so far, with more than 10 million users in the US and Canada. Meta is already seeing gains in its Instagram ad business because Muse helps users organize saved products, which boosts conversion rates for advertisers, CNBC reports. Data from Forter Intelligence shows that Muse recently accounted for 51 percent of all agentic orders, followed by SpaceX's Grok at 24 percent and OpenAI's ChatGPT at 22 percent.

Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the but
paragraphs: Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”

As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.

The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

paragraphs: Officials from the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence briefed staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees on some of what they know about Alice Huang, Megaspeed, and their links to China’s Ministry of State Security, according to the NYT:

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing a surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls, according to Fortune’s Emily Forlini.
The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” said one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion. If Lori leaves, a huge chunk of Jensen’s net worth would potentially transfer to her.

In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

news.title: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
news.title_en: US stocks sell-off deepens as AI trade cracks
news.author: Emily Herbert, Ian Smith, and William Sandlund
news.summary_en: Tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 falls more than 4% as weeks-long slide continues — A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday …
paragraphs: A Wall Street sell-off intensified on Wednesday, pushing the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 down more than 4 per cent, as a brutal unwind of the once-dominant AI trade accelerated.

Shares in Nvidia, which soared on Monday following the shock reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, slid as much as 9 per cent. Rival chipmaker Broadcom lost 7 per cent, while Micron was down 11 per cent.
“The mood is extremely skittish,” said Van Luu, director of global solutions strategy at Russell Investments.

The euphoria sparked by Huang’s return to the top job at Nvidia, America’s biggest chipmaker and the face of the AI boom, had been replaced by a growing realisation “that the scrutiny on the AI ecosystem will [now] intensify”, he added.
The falls briefly pushed the Nasdaq back into a bear market, defined as a fall of 20 per cent from a recent high.
Shares in Claude maker Anthropic, which fell below their $83 listing price for the first time on Tuesday, dropped another 9 per cent on Wednesday to just under $75 as the slump deepened.
In early trading, Anthropic’s market valuation dipped below $1tn for the first time since its listing.
The weakness in tech stocks extends a weeks-long sell-off as doubts mount over whether the historic AI-driven spending boom will pay off and how it will be financed amid climbing interest rates.
In a sign of the souring in risk appetite, traders bought into low-risk US government debt on Wednesday, pushing the 10-year bond yield down 0.08 percentage points to 4.82 per cent.
The Vix index of expected volatility, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, remained elevated at above 35 points, more than double its September low.
“It’s pretty wild out there at the moment,” said Jim Reid, global head of macro research at Deutsche Bank, saying the “risk-off” mood in markets was further stoked by the latest tariff headlines.
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled a number of new tariffs on major trading partners, including the EU, China, Japan and South Korea.
